prose.summary: A carpenter builds, installs and repairs the wooden and timber-framed parts of a building: floors, walls, roofs, stairs, doors, cabinets and the formwork concrete is poured into. People confuse the trade with joinery or cabinetmaking, which happen mostly in a workshop. A carpenter works on site, reads the drawings, and turns them into something square, level and safe to stand on.
prose.day_to_day:
Most days start early, with a look at the drawings and the day's cut list before the site gets loud. The morning is measuring, cutting and fixing: framing a wall, setting joists, hanging a door, or building the formwork for a slab that has to be poured by Thursday. You work from a tape, a level and a drawing, and you check each other's work because a wall that is out of square costs everyone downstream.

The afternoon is often the fiddly part: trimming, fitting skirting and architraves, adjusting a stair stringer, solving the problem the drawing did not anticipate. There is usually a conversation with the site foreman or the client about a change, and a few minutes at the end of the day sharpening tools and squaring away the site so tomorrow starts clean.

The part carpenters mention first is seeing a structure stand where there was nothing in the morning. On a good week you frame a roof, and the moment it goes on is a real one.
prose.work_environment:
This is hands-on, on-site work: construction sites, renovations inside occupied homes, and occasionally a workshop for prefabrication. You are on your feet, lifting, kneeling and working at height, in whatever weather the site has. Almost no postings are remote, for the obvious reason.

Hours usually run early, often from seven, and finish mid-afternoon, with longer stretches when a pour or a handover deadline is close. Winter slows exterior work in colder markets, and Swiss and German postings, which lead this board, often expect a completed apprenticeship (EFZ or Gesellenbrief) and safe-working certification. The social side is close-knit: small crews, direct conversation, and a lot of teaching between the experienced and the new.
prose.getting_in:
The usual door is an apprenticeship: three to four years of paid on-site work with classroom blocks, leading to a recognized qualification (EFZ in Switzerland, Gesellenbrief in Germany, a journeyman card or a level 2 or 3 NVQ elsewhere). Many postings ask for it by name. A meaningful share also accept experience in place of the certificate, especially for site carpentry and formwork, where employers care most that you can read a drawing, cut accurately and work safely at height.

People coming from other trades, from cabinetmaking, or from years of serious renovation work often get in through a labourer or improver role first and prove themselves on the tools. The step that takes longest is not the hiring; it is the first year of speed and accuracy, when you learn to cut once.
prose.ladder:
The first jump is from apprentice or improver to a qualified carpenter trusted to run their own section of a job without supervision. From there it forks. One path is leading: chargehand, then site foreman or working supervisor, where you plan the crew's week, order material and talk to the client. The other is specializing: formwork, timber framing, roofing carpentry, heritage restoration, or fit-out and finishing, each with its own pay premium.

A lot of carpenters go self-employed after five to ten years, either as a subcontractor to builders or with their own renovation clients, and that is where the earnings ceiling really opens. Site management and estimating are the desk-side routes for people who want off the tools without leaving construction.
prose.suits: People who do well here like making physical things well and can see a finished result at the end of the day. Patience with measuring, a tolerance for weather and noise, and the habit of checking your own work matter more than strength. It suits people who prefer a small crew and direct conversation to meetings. The ones who leave usually wanted to be indoors, or wanted work that did not take a toll on knees and shoulders over twenty years, which is a fair reason to plan a move into supervising or estimating in time.
prose.misconceptions: The outside view is that carpentry is unskilled labour. Most of the job is geometry, reading drawings and sequencing work so that trades do not block each other, and a good carpenter is often the person on site who catches the mistake in the plans before it is built. The other misconception is that it is a dead end; site management, estimating, and self-employment are all well-worn paths out of it.
prose.tools: Postings name the fundamentals: reading construction drawings, framing and formwork, and safe working at height, along with power tools (circular saws, nail guns, routers) and the hand tools you own yourself. Formwork systems (Doka, Peri) show up in Swiss and German postings, and a driving licence appears often enough to count as a requirement for site work. Basic CAD literacy is a plus for fit-out and prefabrication roles.

steps.how: A labourer or improver role with a carpentry crew is the fastest way to find out if you like it, and it is where most apprenticeships are offered.
Three to four years, paid, on site with classroom blocks. In Switzerland and Germany it is the expected route; elsewhere a union or college programme does the same job.
Working at height, scaffolding, first aid and site safety certification. Cheap, quick, and asked for by name in a lot of postings.
The carpenters who progress are the ones who can take a plan and a section and see the sequence. Ask for it on every job.

steps.do: Pick a specialty by year three
steps.how: Formwork, framing, roofing or finishing each pay differently and lead to different crews. Decide with your knees in mind.

prose.who_qualifies: Cabinetmakers and joiners move across easily; the precision carries and only the site habits are new. Roofers, scaffolders and formwork labourers already know the site side and mostly need the measuring and finishing skills. People from furniture making, set construction and serious renovation work also convert well, usually through an improver role first.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows how much the crew you land in shapes the job: a good foreman who teaches is worth more than a pay rise in the first two years. It also cannot tell you what the work does to your body over decades, which is why the smart carpenters plan the move into supervising, estimating or their own business before they need to.

industries.name: Residential construction and renovation
industries.note: The bulk of the postings, from new builds to loft conversions. Steady, local, and where most self-employed carpenters work.

industries.name: Commercial and civil construction
industries.note: Formwork, structural timber and fit-out on larger sites. More structure, more safety paperwork, often better pay.

industries.name: Timber frame and prefabrication
industries.note: Growing in Switzerland, Germany and the Nordics: factory-built panels and modules assembled on site.

industries.name: Heritage and restoration
industries.note: Traditional joints and materials on older buildings. A smaller, well-paid niche that rewards patience.

specializations.name: Formwork carpenter
specializations.why: Builds the moulds for concrete. In demand on every large site and paid for precision under time pressure.

specializations.name: Timber framer
specializations.why: Structural frames, roofs and increasingly engineered timber. The skill that keeps rising with sustainable building.

specializations.name: Finish and fit-out carpenter
specializations.why: Doors, stairs, trim and interiors. The most visible work and the most client contact.

specializations.name: Site foreman
specializations.why: Runs the crew and the programme. The usual step for carpenters who want to lead without leaving site.

pros: You see what you built at the end of every day, and it stays built.
Demand is steady across markets and the apprenticeship is paid, so you earn while you qualify.
Self-employment is a realistic path with a real earnings ceiling after a few years.
The skills transfer across countries better than most trades, with recognized qualifications in Switzerland, Germany and beyond.
cons: It is physical work in real weather, and it asks something of your body over the years.
Early starts and deadline weeks around pours and handovers are part of the rhythm.
Pay in the first apprenticeship years is modest, and the fastest rises come from specializing or going self-employed.
Site work depends on the construction cycle, so slow winters and slow years happen.

faq.q: Do I need an apprenticeship to become a carpenter?
faq.a: In Switzerland and Germany, almost always: postings ask for the EFZ or Gesellenbrief by name. Elsewhere it is the most common route but not the only one; plenty of site carpenters got in as labourers or improvers and proved themselves on the tools, then picked up the qualification later.

faq.q: How long does it take to become a qualified carpenter?
faq.a: Three to four years through an apprenticeship, earning as you go. Reaching the point where a foreman trusts you with your own section of a job usually takes another year or two of speed and accuracy.

Look at the pay section above: it is computed from the postings on our board that state a salary, by level and by country, and it refreshes nightly. The short version is that qualified site carpenters in Switzerland and Germany earn well above the apprenticeship years, and specialists and the self-employed earn more again.

faq.q: Is carpentry a good career if I want to run my own business later?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the trades where that path is most worn. After five to ten years many carpenters subcontract to builders or take on their own renovation clients. Estimating and site management are the other routes for people who want off the tools.

faq.q: What is the difference between a carpenter and a joiner?
faq.a: A joiner makes things in a workshop, such as windows, doors and staircases, with fine tolerances and machinery. A carpenter installs and builds on site, from framing and roofs to fitting what the joiner made. Many people do both over a career, and the skills carry across.

responsibilities: Read construction drawings and set out the work: levels, lines and dimensions on site.
Frame walls, floors and roofs in timber, and build formwork for concrete.
Install doors, windows, stairs, skirting, trim and fitted joinery to a finish standard.
Cut, shape and fix timber accurately with hand and power tools, and keep them sharp and safe.
Work at height safely, on scaffolds and roofs, with the right certification.
Coordinate with other trades and the foreman so the sequence of work does not block anyone.
Check your own work for square, plumb and level before the next trade builds on it.

levels.title: Apprentice
levels.focus: Learn the tools, the drawings and site safety while working alongside qualified carpenters. Paid, with classroom blocks.

levels.title: Qualified carpenter
levels.focus: Run your own section of a job without supervision: framing, formwork or finishing to standard and on time.

levels.title: Specialist or chargehand
levels.focus: Either the deep end of one specialty (formwork, framing, heritage) or leading a small crew day to day.

levels.title: Foreman, estimator or self-employed
levels.focus: Plan the programme, price the work and talk to clients, on site or in your own business.
